Anatomia unui alibi

Ashley Elston, Constantin Dumitru-Palcus (Translator)

3.76
209,227 ratings22,492 reviews
Rate this book
Buze roșii, pantofi de designer, un Negroni sorbit în barul Chantilly’s. Camille Bayliss a fost văzută de toată lumea. Doar că nu era ea, ci Aubrey Price.

Camille Bayliss are viața perfectă: e căsătorită cu Ben, un avocat de succes, și vine dintr-o familie foarte înstărită din Louisiana. Aparențele însă sunt înșelătoare. Camille simte că Ben ascunde de ani întregi secrete murdare, dar nu poate găsi nicio dovadă, pentru că soțul ei îi urmărește fiecare mișcare.

Aubrey Price e bântuită de noaptea care i-a schimbat viața cu zece ani în urmă și e convinsă că Benjamin Bayliss știe mai multe decât lasă să se vadă. Aubrey știe că sunt mai multe căi prin care poate afla adevărul, iar una dintre ele e femeia care caută la fel de multă răzbunare ca și ea.

Aubrey și Camille pun la cale un plan. Timp de douăsprezece ore, Aubrey îi va lua locul lui Camille. În acest timp, Camille îl va spiona pe Ben, iar împreună vor obține răspunsurile pe care le caută cu disperare.

Numai că, în dimineața următoare, bărbatul e găsit fără viață.

Ambele femei au nevoie de un alibi impecabil, însă doar una dintre ele îl are. Un singur pas greșit și întregul plan se prăbușește...

About the author

Ashley Elston

9 books10.6k followers
Ashley Elston worked for many years as a wedding photographer before turning her hand to writing. She lives in Louisiana with her husband and three sons. Elston has written six young adult novels. FIRST LIE WINS, her adult debut, was a number one New York Times bestseller and was selected as a Reese’s Book Club pick.

Yun
684 reviews43.1k followers
February 10, 2026
I like twists and turns as much as the next thriller-loving gal. I mean, who wouldn't want to be surprised and stunned and stupefied to within an inch of their life? But in order for the twists to deliver, they have to make sense within the story and its characters. And unfortunately, that didn't really happen here.

Initially, Anatomy of an Alibi seemed off to a good start. We are introduced to Camille and Aubrey, one trying to get out of her marriage and the other impersonating her to give her the alibi she needs to achieve her goal. But then as the story progressed and the twists started piling on, it became ever more convoluted and absurd, and before I knew it, I was tuning out.

The problem is that the story lacked believable and fleshed out characters to anchor all the mayhem. Everyone in here came across as flat and nondescript, there to further the plot along but not much else. When every character is bland and everything they do and say is generic, it's hard to get into the story.

And the sheer number of characters was bewildering. As more and more of them were introduced, I could feel my eyebrows migrating towards my hairline. By the time Aubrey's four roommates came into the picture, each of whom was clearly put there to serve a very specific purpose, I just couldn't take it seriously anymore.

I kept waiting for the moment when I would buy into the story and really care—about the characters, about the plotlines, about the twists—but it just never happened. I'm pretty sure if I had quit the story midway and never found out the conclusion, I wouldn't even have shrugged. When everything is random and all the characters interchangeable, what does it really matter what happens to one when it could've easily happened to another?

And if I'm being honest, I wasn't wild about the writing either. I noticed it in First Lie Wins (Ashley Elston's adult debut), but the superior story there covered for that deficiency. Here, it was on full display. The author favors present tense, which can add a sense of immediacy to the tale, but with the downside that it can also make the writing feel simplistic and forced.

I went into this with high expectations. Ashley Elston's previous book was a standout thriller that delivered both a unique storyline and all the thrills. So to have this one fall short is particularly disappointing.

That all sounds super negative, but it wasn't that bad of a read. It certainly goes by fast enough if you're looking to wile away a few hours. But it prioritizes its twists over everything else, and at the end of the day, it's just hard to come away feeling satisfied with a story like that.

4.5/5 ★

🚨 Warning: Clear your schedule before starting this one because from the very beginning it’s impossible to put down.

In Anatomy of an Alibi, Aubrey Price impersonates Camille Bayliss for one night so Camille can secretly spy on her husband Ben Bayliss, who she suspects is hiding dangerous secrets. When Ben is found murdered the next morning, both women are trapped in a deadly game where only one of them has an airtight alibi, and a single mistake could expose everything.

Ashley Elston is quickly becoming one of my favorite mystery/thriller authors. This was even better than First Lie Wins (4.5 ★), in my opinion.

By the end of chapter two, I was completely hooked. This book is so fast paced and the mystery is so well structured that I flew through it.

Every character in this book felt complex, intelligent, and sneaky. Each one has their own agenda and motivations, all tightly intertwined, making it incredibly engaging to unravel the story from the different perspectives.

My only complaint is that with the story being as fast paced as it was, I was hoping for a twist that fully shocked me. That didn’t quite happen. There were definitely twists throughout the story, but I guessed all but one. The one I didn’t guess came somewhat out of nowhere and left me more confused than surprised. I still think it has twists that will shock a lot of readers, especially those who read less in this genre.

If you enjoyed Kill for Me, Kill for You (4.5 ★), The Kind Worth Killing (3.5 ★), The Intern (4.5 ★), and/or First Lie Wins, I strongly recommend this one. While it didn’t feel identical to any of them, those were the books that immediately came to mind while reading.

Overall, this was an intense mystery and high-stakes thriller that kept me hooked from start to finish.

Hands down, Ashley Elston did it again. My first Elston read was the adorable YA rom-com 10 Blind Dates—soft, sweet, total swoon fuel. I loved her voice. Then she knocked the wind out of me with Reese’s Book Club pick First Lie Wins, proving the same writer who delivers cinnamon-roll romance can also craft my favorite thriller of last year. I bowed. I whistled. I applauded. And now? She’s back with another twisty rocket ride that had me literally perched on the edge of my seat begging the Good Books Gods (aka Penguin/Viking) for an ARC. Wish granted—thank you!—and I was hooked from page one.

The hook (no spoilers)

Two women, one dangerous bargain, and a dead man at the center of it all.

Aubrey (26) tends bar, shares a place with ex-cons because rent is brutal, and still aches for justice ten years after her parents were killed in a hit-and-run.

Camille is Old-Money Louisiana—sugarcane legacy, glittering parties, and a marriage to powerful attorney Benjamin Bayliss, who controls everything from her schedule to her smile.

Their lives collide when a mysterious flash drive may hold the key to the driver who killed Aubrey’s parents—and Benjamin might be the only one with access to the truth. Camille wants out of her gilded cage. Aubrey wants answers. So they make a risky swap that lets Camille vanish for a few days while Aubrey “plays Camille” and snoops.

And then Benjamin is found stabbed.

Suddenly everyone’s a suspect: Hank (the law partner on the verge of being pushed out), the ever-convenient spouse, and yes—Aubrey, the stand-in with no alibi and her real name and address written on a slip of paper in Ben’s pocket. Was Ben investigating her? Protecting her? Or feeding her to wolves? Meanwhile, Camille’s formidable Everett family hums with secrets, and her brother is tangled in more than he admits. Trust is a currency everyone spends; truth is the one thing nobody can afford.

Why it works

Elston builds a smart, propulsive puzzle that keeps your brain happily sprinting. From the first chapters you’re juggling three delicious questions:

Who killed Ben?

Who killed Aubrey’s parents?

What’s on the flash drive?

I even made a clue board (yes, with string) and still only nailed two out of three. The third answer hit me like a door in a hurricane—clean, earned, and devilishly planted. Points to Ms. Elston for the fair-play misdirection and those “ohhhh” breadcrumbs hiding in plain sight.

Vibe check

Pacing: Lightning fast without sacrificing character.

Tone: Legal-world intrigue, high-stakes domestic tension, found-family grit.

Characters: Women who refuse to stay small, men whose power looks different up close, and side players who actually matter.

Twists: Sharp, surprising, and—praise be—logical.

Final thoughts

Hold your breath. Go in blind. Cook up your theories. Prepare to be sucker-punched by reveals and then grin because the clues were right there. This is an unputdownable, high-octane mystery that rockets straight onto my Top 10 Thrillers of the Year list. Ashley Elston is now an automatic-read thriller queen for me.

Huge thanks to NetGalley and Viking / Penguin, Pamela Dorman Books for the ARC of one of my most anticipated 2026 releases in exchange for my honest thoughts. I’m already counting the days until I can shove this into everyone’s hands.

Anatomy of an Alibi by Ashley Elston

We get a LOT of lessons in how to set up alibis, all the way to the last sentence of the book, and it's fun watching things happen in a mixed up timeline which had me perplexed at times. Camille Bayliss and Aubrey Price are nothing alike but there is a short time in this story when they are the same person. Wealthy socialite Camille Bayliss needed an alibi and she got one, which is a very good thing because someone is dead in her house and she's going to be a prime suspect. Good thing she was no where around...or was she?

Aubrey needs to know what Benjamin Bayliss knows and she has a lot of friends who can help her get the information she needs. It's nice to have friends in low places. I really like Aubrey and her friends, living their hard times together, watching out for each other, more a family than blood and marriage for some people.

All of what is going on now started years ago with an accident, a possibly wrong conviction, and a chance that the truth could come out. The truth could ruin people, but then maybe those people need ruining. This is a tightly wound story, told out of timeline order, and it was enjoyable to the very end. The last sentence is great and makes it clear that some things may never be over.

“The tricky part about the anatomy of an alibi is not just that someone will vouch that you were somewhere else when a crime was committed-but that the “someone else” is believable…”

Camille Bayliss appears to have it all- she’s married to hotshot lawyer Ben and is the daughter of a well connected and powerful Louisiana family. But, Camille wants out and her Prenup is going to require that she obtains proof of Ben’s wrongdoings if she is to leave unscathed. The problem is that she can’t find that proof because Ben tracks her every move.

Aubrey Price is convinced that Benjamin Bayliss knows something about the night that her parents were killed by a drunk driver-and that the wrong man may be in prison for the crime. And, when Camille comes to see her at the bar where she is working with an accusation of her own-she realizes that she may have just found a way to get to the truth.

Everyone at Chantilly’s Bar notices the woman who comes into the bar in her designer shoes 👠 who orders a Negroni (of all things!) to sip on with her red painted lips. 👄. Her bar tab will say it is Camille Bayliss.

BUT IT WAS ACTUALLY AUBREY PRICE.

Aubrey and Camille had hatched a plan where for twelve hours, Aubrey will take Camille’s place, while Camille spies on Ben, and hopefully obtains the answers that each woman seeks.

EXCEPT the next morning, Ben is found murdered, and only ONE of the women has an airtight alibi.

Was Aubrey set up to be the scapegoat?

NOTHING is what it seems.

The story will unfold through the alternating first person POV’s of Camille, her lawyer Hank, and Aubrey in the present day, and occasionally, from Ben’s POV ten years ago.

Last January, Ashley Elston burst onto the scene when she transitioned from writing YA books to the Adult Thriller market with her book FIRST LIE WINS (5 ⭐️) And, while I’m going to give the edge to that one, this sophomore effort was almost just as good! Review for First Lie Wins: https://www.goodreads.com/review/show...

And, you will know just HOW apropos this title is when you read the VERY LAST SENTENCE. (No peeking!)🫣

I was hooked from the very entertaining opening scene and I just had to know who COULD and who COULD NOT be trusted.

It’s been awhile since I have read a really CLEVER, FAST PACED thriller and I am thrilled to report that if you have been looking for one too, this is it!

4.5 stars ⭐️ rounded up!

A buddy read with DeAnn and Ceecee! Be sure to watch for their reviews!

3.5⭐️ rounded up because it kept me entertained.

Camille Bayliss is certain her husband, Ben, is hiding something, but his constant surveillance makes it impossible to gather proof. Aubrey Price has her own reasons for wanting answers, believing Ben was tied to the tragedy that upended her life ten years ago. When the two women meet, they devise a dangerous plan: Aubrey will impersonate Camille for twelve hours while Camille searches for the truth.

Then Ben is murdered, and only one of them has an airtight alibi.

While the audiobook narration by Macleod Andrews, Saskia Maarleveld (a favorite of mine), Amanda Stripling, and Dan Bittner was excellent, I recommend reading this one with your eyes. With multiple POVs and four timelines to follow, you may find yourself going back to reread certain parts once the truth begins to come to light.

This was such a fun one to discuss with Kelsey, and our theories kept changing as the story progressed. We both grew attached to two of the side characters and found ourselves hoping they would not end up being the culprit.

This story is a tangled web with everyone’s lives intersecting. It is fast paced and compulsively readable, making it all too easy to say “just one more chapter.”

My biggest issue was the final twist, which didn’t quite land and left me more confused than shocked, and not in a good way. I’d expand on why this fell short of a four star read, but that would risk spoilers. Even so, it remained an entertaining read that I can easily recommend.

Another great buddy read with my friend Kelsey. Be sure to check out her review as well to see what she thought of it.

‘Alibi: A defense offered by a defendant who claims that he or she was at some other place at the time of the commission of the crime and therefore did not commit the crime charged.’

If you loved Ashley Elston’s, First Lie Wins, you’ll feel right at home here and honestly? I might’ve enjoyed this one even more.

Ashley Elston does what she does best, sharp pacing, morally grey characters, and a plot that quietly tightens around you until you realise you’re holding your breath. First Lie Wins was clever and compulsive, but Anatomy of an Alibi feels a little darker, a little more psychological, and even more confident in its twists.

The premise is instantly juicy, two women, a dangerous secret, and an identity swap that seems smart right up until it absolutely isn’t. Camille Bayliss suspects her powerful husband is hiding something sinister. Aubrey Price has her own unresolved past. They make a deal, step into each other’s lives for just one day…and then a murder blows everything apart.

From there, it becomes a delicious game of alibis, half truths, and carefully curated lies. Elston leans hard into the idea that truth doesn’t matter nearly as much as what can be proven and watching the characters scramble to control the narrative is incredibly addictive.

The dual perspectives work beautifully, the tension never lets up, and just when you think you’ve figured out where it’s going, Elston pivots. Again…and again. It’s the kind of book that makes you suspicious of everyone, including yourself.

While First Lie Wins was a blast, Anatomy of an Alibi felt more layered to me, sharper, colder, and a touch more ruthless. A psychological thriller that trusts its readers and isn’t afraid to let its characters be messy, selfish, and deeply human.

Smart, twisty, and quietly brutal, this one stuck with me long after the final page.

I Highly Recommend.

Thank you Headline Publishing for my early readers copy.

Camille is from a wealthy family and married to prominent Baton Rouge defense lawyer Ben Bayliss. Her vision for the future doesn’t align with her husband’s and she secretly wants out, but she needs to trigger a bad behavior clause in their pre-nup to justify the divorce. She has to dig up some dirt on him, which is hard to do when he digitally tracks her every move.

Aubrey Price works in a bar and lives with a ragtag group of individuals with various criminal talents. After losing her parents in a tragic car crash ten years ago, this is her de facto family. When Camille crosses paths with her and asks Aubrey to pretend to be her on a solo trip to another town so that she can stay behind and investigate Ben, Aubrey agrees.

Everything goes to plan until Ben is found dead. Now one woman has the appearance of an airtight alibi and the other is in deep doo-doo. Will Aubrey end up on the wrong side of this plan?

It’s a great premise, fantastic writing, perfectly orchestrated plotting, well-developed characters, an intriguing Louisiana setting, and all those twists and turns that make thriller-lovers' hearts beat faster. To top it all off, this was an immersion read with my Kindle and the audio, and the narrators were all amazing, including one of my personal favorites, Saskia Maarleveld.

There’s literally no good reason I can come up with for me not to have loved this book and given it 5 stars like so many other friends, especially after Elston blew me away with her debut thriller First Lie Wins, yet here I am. I’m not sure what didn’t click as well for me this time, but it was an issue from the very beginning and never really let up.

I suspect this is just an issue of me not being a big fan of stories involving wealthy families who misuse their influence. I found it harder to connect to the characters in this book, though I did like Aubrey and her housemates - especially Deacon - and also Ben’s law partner Hank. While I enjoyed the story well enough and commend the skill with which Elston writes a thriller, I just didn’t LOVE it the way I wanted to. Perhaps the winter storm outside my windows is making me gloomy!

Having said all of that, it’s with NO hesitation that I recommend this book to my fellow thriller-lovers. There’s a long line of them who loved this one as much or even more than her last one, so please read their reviews before deciding whether to try this.

★★★ ½

2.5 stars —- I was looking forward to reading “Anatomy of an Alibi’ after really enjoying the first book I read by Ashley Elston, “The First Lie Wins.’ However, “Anatomy” was another book that didn’t check all of the boxes for me. The writing and plot were efficient and tight, but unfortunately, I spent most of my time bored and checking to see how many pages I had left to read. I spent the whole book trying to get into the story more but much of the plot felt forced and the characters just didn’t seem real to me based on their actions and behavior. The book is told from many different perspectives which probably didn’t help me get invested in the characters. The story centers around Aubrey and Camille — two women who become bonded when Camille falsely accuses Aubrey of having an affair with her lawyer husband, Ben. Camille had become suspicious after finding Aubrey’s personal information on a napkin in Ben’s briefcase. Ben is a controlling spouse who his wife suspects of wanting to divorce her so she attempts to flip the tables on him by using Aubrey to pose as her so she can spy on Ben to get evidence that will void their prenuptial agreement. Oh, and did I mention Aubrey just happens to be the orphaned daughter of two people killed in a hit and run accident from years ago that Ben provided the key alibi for a suspect in the deaths that led to another person being charged and convicted for the deaths. Now the bad news: this is just the first 50 pages of the novel; the book gets much more convoluted and far-reaching for the remainder of the book —280 pages or so. 3.5 stars.

'This is the tricky part. It’s not just the anatomy of an alibi—having someone vouch that you were somewhere else when the crime was committed—but it’s the psychology of it: that that someone is believable.'

After thoroughly enjoying "First Lie Wins" last year, I was incredibly excited to discover that this author had written another thriller. It met all my expectations for entertainment and intrigue.

The mystery was intricately constructed and well executed, making it engaging to follow the characters as they uncovered various secrets. There were no noticeable plot holes, and the entire storyline was coherent and logically consistent.

Camille was my favorite among the two protagonists. She was portrayed as a spoiled, wealthy woman who primarily cared about her money. I enjoyed being inside her point of view because she was unapologetically focused on her goal of divorcing her husband, Ben, without risking her financial stability. I respected her clear sense of purpose and her determination. She was relatable to an extent, especially in her desire to escape a controlling marriage.

I also appreciated the close bond Camille shared with her brother, Silas. It was easy to relate to their relationship because, despite fighting with my brother, we know we can count on each other when we need to.

On the other hand, Aubrey was a significant disappointment. I found her and her group of friends unlikable, reminiscent of a stereotypical goofy gang like the Scooby-Doo crew. They seemed to believe they were the smartest, which was frustrating because, in reality, they were just as ignorant as anyone else. Her primary character trait was her status as an orphan, and she repeatedly brought this up throughout the story. By the end, her constant mentions became tiresome, and I couldn't care less about her past. Additionally, she often thought of Camille as less intelligent than her, but honestly, both were equally foolish. Her chapters also felt slow and dull, dragging down parts of the narrative.

Hank stood out as the most impressive character, distinguished by his sharp attention to detail and calm demeanor in stressful situations. I always appreciate a clever, quick-thinking character in thrillers, and Hank fits this mold perfectly. I also loved how gentle and protective he was towards Camille.

Finally, Ben was perhaps the most intriguing and complex figure in the story. I found myself liking him, largely because the author charmingly portrayed him, making it easy for readers to understand why he was such an effective lawyer. His ability to spin stories in his favor was convincing, and I was immersed in his perspective. Was he a good person? No. Was he a bad person? Also no. He was simply a man trying to escape poverty, seizing an opportunity when it appeared, and becoming corrupted by power along the way. I wish the narrative had included more point-of-view chapters from him, as those were the most captivating and held my attention more. His compulsive need for control, over Camille's life and all the other aspects of his life was unsettling, revealing the depths of his obsession.

In conclusion, this was a well-crafted and highly entertaining thriller.

After First Lie Wins became my favorite book of the year in 2024, I knew I needed to get my hands on Elston’s next novel as soon as I could. Let me tell you, with Anatomy of an Alibi she cemented her talent for writing twisty, unputdownable thrillers in no uncertain terms. A brilliant yet complicated puzzle of multiple timelines told from multiple POVs, it was a fun, wild ride of long-buried secrets and manipulative lies. You see, on top of one heck of a dysfunctional family, the two women at the center of the action were matched wit for wit in this epic game of cat-and-mouse. Don’t get me wrong, they weren’t the only ones playing for keeps as the web of well-hidden schemes were unraveled thread by thread as this complex plot flew by in a wink of an eye. Compelling, intense, and beyond ingenious, it was everything I look for in a one-sitting read.

All said and done, despite an incredibly intricate plot which required a ton of focus to keep my eye on the ball, I couldn’t put this book down until I knew all the whos, whats, and whys. With cliffhangers galore and a storyline with a definite Hitchcockian vibe, I was thrown more than once by one of the “HOLY S***!?!” twists. Coming in hot and heavy after the halfway point, I even dropped my book in surprise near the end. After all, thanks to a blindingly fast pace and a group of highly suspicious characters, there was no telling who the killer really was until it was laid at my feet. That’s right. Even I didn’t know the truth until the heart-pounding reveal. Even better, if you prefer a bit of depth to your thrillers, this one had that as well. Exploring class, identity, and trust, it was a humdinger of a read that will take a while to get over. Rating of 4.5 stars.

BRIEF BLURB:

Please oh please go into this one as blind as you can! I mean, even the publisher-provided synopsis gave just a bit too much away. All you need to know before diving in is what I’m about to tell you in the following blurb…

A wealthy trophy wife named Camille Bayliss suspects that something suspicious is going on in her marriage to Ben. Hoping to get to the bottom of it, she confronts bartender Aubrey Price about some information she has found that seems to connect her to Ben. The only problem is that Camille is wrong. Sort of. Hoping to catch him out, they plan a devious scheme. The only problem is that both of them are hiding things from one another. At least, that was their only problem…until Ben ends up dead. With their lies spinning out of control, they have to rush to work out who killed Ben and why before one of them ends up behind bars. After all, only one of them has the perfect alibi…

Thank you Ashley Elston, Pamela Dorman Books, and NetGalley for my complimentary digital and physical copies. All opinions are my own.

Twisty. Frenetic. Occasionally exhausting.

“Alibi: A defense offered by a defendant who claims that he or she was at some other place at the time of the commission of the crime and therefore did not commit the crime charged.” — Louisiana State Bar Association

Let us breathe in the last part of that statement.

“…and therefore, did not commit the crime charged.”

Hmm. How, exactly, should readers interpret that?

This novel sets out to examine the anatomy of an alibi—a meticulous, piece-by-piece construction of a defense meant to prove someone wasn’t there when the crime occurred. And that is, more or less, the story readers are following.

But first, readers will find themselves asking: what crime—and who is it really about?

Ben, a successful attorney is dead. Or at least, we as readers, know a murder has occurred. From there, suspicion spreads quickly. Was it Camille, his wife, worn down by his controlling nature? Hank, his business partner? Aubrey, whose past feels carefully guarded? Or someone else entirely, protecting secrets that run deeper than Ben’s murder?

An alibi must be built—but why? To get away with murder? Or to conceal something far more complicated?

Told through alternating points of view, the story immediately pulls readers into a compelling mystery where everyone feels like a suspect—but not always for the same reason. The tension lies not just in who committed the crime, but in whose alibi can be trusted, what crime this story is truly about, and whether justice will ultimately prevail. (No spoilers from me.)

And this is where the novel both succeeds and stumbles.

The twists come fast and furious—so many, in fact, that readers may begin to feel a bit of narrative whiplash. With an ever-expanding cast of characters and constant reversals, the story sometimes feels less like a carefully plotted mystery and more like a runaway roller coaster. Intriguing? Yes. Overwhelming at times? Also, yes.

By the end, readers may find themselves wanting resolution—and perhaps a moment to steady themselves—rather than yet another sharp turn.

A gripping premise with strong intrigue, but one that could have benefited from some restraint. That said, I may be an outlier—so I encourage readers to explore other reviews and perspectives before deciding if this whirlwind mystery is right for them.

⭐️⭐️⭐️.5 stars, rounded down.
